Google says it can build data centers the right way. Some experts and residents are skeptical
headlines.summary: Google says its Minnesota AI data center will add clean energy to the grid and protect ratepayers. Experts question whether grid upgrades are needed.
headlines.article_text: How AI data centers are reshaping America's aging grid Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points AI data centers are poised to drive North America’s electricity demand growth over the next decade, fueling a massive grid buildout. Google and Xcel Energy say their proposed 780-megawatt data center in Minnesota will upgrade the grid with cleaner power without shifting infrastructure costs onto existing customers. But experts say much of that buildout could be avoided and warn that utilities have a financial incentive to keep building. In this article GOOGL SPCX XEL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 11:44 11:44 The race to power AI data centers is reshaping America's electric grid Tech If there's one thing most Americans can agree on, it's that they don't want a data center in their backyard. A Gallup survey conducted in March found that 71% of Americans opposed the construction of a data center in their local area. Chief among their concerns: energy usage. Half of Americans surveyed by Pew Research Center in July and August said data centers would be mostly bad for the environment and for household energy costs. Now Google is betting that a massive AI data center can help finance a cleaner, more reliable power grid. Its proposed deal with Xcel Energy would add more wind, solar and battery capacity than the data center is expected to use. Under the agreement, Google would help pay for the added capacity and continue paying, even if it doesn't use all of the power. Google's bet that AI can finance a cleaner grid Pine Island, Minnesota, is a small town of about 4,000 residents an hour southeast of Minneapolis. Google hopes that its new 780-megawatt data center plan will build goodwill with the Pine Island community and keep the company on track to meet its goal of operating on carbon-free energy, 24 hours a day, seven days a week by 2030 . Google — whose cloud business powers its own Gemini AI and brought in nearly $25 billion in second-quarter revenue, an 82% increase from a year earlier — says it has found a model for doing this the right way. The company plans to finance the addition of 1,400 megawatts of wind, 200 megawatts of solar and 300 megawatts of battery storage to Xcel's grid. Those additions amount to more than the capacity of the data center itself, which Google said is because wind and solar do not generate energy at all times. Xcel Energy said the new power will serve all customers in the local area, not just Google. Xcel also said the upgrades will help advance the local grid's carbon-free energy supply. The proposed agreement between Google and Xcel includes minimum demand charges and exit fees, which Google says will keep the company on the hook for the infrastructure being built on its behalf, even if the AI boom cools. Google will pay for at least 75% of its contracted capacity, even if it uses less, and would owe up to eight years' worth of those minimum demand charges if it terminates the agreement early. "Nobody wants to have a big buildout and then have nowhere for that power to go and nobody to pay for that power," said Amanda Rome, executive vice president and chief customer officer at Xcel Energy. "That's where these protections come in." The agreement between Google and Xcel Energy is pending approval by the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission. Data centers are driving a historic power buildout New data centers will account for "most" of the projected increase in electricity demand over the next decade, according to the North American Electric Reliability Corporation, a nonprofit regulator. The Department of Energy under President Joe Biden reported that more than 70% of U.S. transmission lines and power transformers were at least 25 years old and found that the cheapest ways of meeting future demand would require the nation's transmission system to more than double in size by 2050 . But hyperscalers argue that they can finance badly needed grid upgrades while also making the grid cleaner and more reliable. "The timing of this industrial revolution couldn't be more perfect," said Amanda Peterson Corio, Google's global head of energy and power. "It's right at the time when we needed capital to fix aging infrastructure in the United States." Could data centers use the grid as is? Jigar Shah, a partner at Multiplier, a consulting firm that helps clean energy startups go public, said data center operators could be constructing smaller facilities in places where the grid already has unused capacity. That would minimize the need to build — and pay for — new generation or transmission equipment. "If you fit the load growth that the data centers want into the existing grid, everybody's rates go down by a lot," said Shah. That's because the existing grid has enormous fixed costs from the infrastructure already in place: power plants, transmission lines, substations. If one new customer comes onto the grid and pays a large slice of that, everyone else's bills go down. "And so the question really is, why are people not doing these 25-megawatt data centers? Why are they doing 1,000-megawatt data centers? And it turns out people are just lazy," Shah said. "They're like, well, it's easier for me to contract one data center that's one gigawatt in size than figuring out how to do something on the order of 40 data centers that are 25 megawatts each." Industry watchdogs also warn of another reason that utilities often prefer to build new infrastructure, rather than make more use out of their existing grid. "When [utilities] build something new, they fund part of that investment with dollars from their investors on Wall Street, and they enjoy incredibly high, exorbitant returns on those investments, typically around 10%," said David Pomerantz, executive director at the Energy and Policy Institute, a utility watchdog agency. Building a data center that fits neatly into an existing grid provides little opportunity for a utility to make new money. What if a hyperscaler offers to pay for those grid investments? "One way to leverage data centers to lower people's bills is for data centers to provide that capital at much cheaper rates than the utility," said Pomerantz. "But that's a big problem for the utility. And this fight is actually already emerging." Still, Shah said, the Google/Xcel project in Minnesota is a good example of a data center project acting as a catalyst for newer, greener technology. "Google came in and said, well, here's a new way of doing things, using new technologies. How about we do it that way? And then that helps ratepayers. And the utility was like, yeah, that makes a lot of sense." The defendant, Abdulrahman Alfozan , communicated with the Saudi royal as recently as Oct. 5 — four days before he was arrested, the U.S. Attorney's Office in San Francisco said in the filing, which requests that he be detained without bail. Prosecutors did not identify the Saudi royal or say in the filing how Alfozan, who then was working as an engineer at OpenAI, knew that person. "Among other things, the individual [the royal family member] told the defendant [Alfozan] that an artificial intelligence initiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and wanted the defendant to join it," prosecutors wrote in their filing. "In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,' indicating he agreed," prosecutors wrote. "The individual repeatedly tried to recruit the defendant and asked when he planned to leave OpenAI," prosecutors wrote. "At the time, the defendant said he wouldn't leave until his stock vested." The filing does not say that the Saudi royal directed Alfozan to install a recording device at OpenAI or steal information from that AI giant. Alfozan, who lives near the San Francisco airport, is a venture partner at Raed Ventures , a Saudi venture capital firm. Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, joined the firm as a venture partner in 2025. In their filing Sunday, prosecutors did not mention that prince by name or say that the unidentified royal who communicated with Alfozan had ties to Raed. The recording device planted at OpenAI's office, according to the Department of Justice. Courtesy: U.S. Department of Justice Prosecutors in the same filing said the Saudi government and then, shortly afterward, a member of the Saudi military booked separate flights for Alfozan's wife, Lujain Alassaf, and their three-month-old son to fly out of the United States after his Oct. 9 arrest upended plans for the three of them to fly as a family to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12. The wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar, on Oct. 10 on a business-class flight paid for by the unidentified member of the Saudi military, the filing said. The filing asks that a judge order Alfozan, 35, detained without bail when he appears in U.S. District Court in San Francisco on Monday morning. Alfozan has been in jail since his arrest on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted. OpenAI fired him after his arrest. Alfozan's lawyer, William Pernik, in a separate filing asked that the defendant be released with home detention and GPS monitoring, and a bond co-signed by others, and "supported by the written undertaking of the Consulate General of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia." The Saudi embassy in Washington, D.C., has not responded to CNBC's requests for comment on Alfozan since his arrest was announced on Oct. 13. Prosecutors said that in the days around the time that Alfozan allegedly installed the recording device on Sept. 28 in the back of a television in the conference room, "OpenAI executives met with government officials in that very room." "Defendant's conduct could pose a danger to the national security of the United States," prosecutors said in the filing. FBI Director Kash Patel, when Alfozan's arrest was announced, said he allegedly concealed the recording device to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's artificial intelligence technology. Prosecutors in their new filing also argued that Alfozan is a flight risk because of his access to "ample resources ... and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government that has (i) no extradition treaty with the United States; (ii) limitless resources; and (iii) the ability to provide extraordinary travel assistance, including based on similar circumstances in this District," the filing said. "He has the connections needed not only to flee, but to build a new life in Saudi Arabia. The Court should order the defendant detained pending trial," prosecutors wrote. Alfozan has spent about 15 years in the United States, working at various tech companies, including Meta, and obtaining a master's degree from the University of California, Berkeley in 2025. He is a legal permanent resident of the United States and has applied to become a naturalized citizen. For his most recent job, as an OpenAI engineer, Alfozan was hired in July 2025 with an annual base salary of $325,000, which was later increased to $385,000, prosecutors said in their filing. He also received a new hire equity grant of $2.2 million in profit participating units, the filing said. Alfozan planned to take two months of parental leave after the birth of his son, according to the filing. He and his family were scheduled to fly one-way to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12. "On or about September 28, 2026 — about two weeks before their scheduled flight—the defendant inserted a surreptitious audio recording device into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive OpenAI conference room, where the device remained for at least multiple days," the filing said. The conference room is frequently used for "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships," the filing said. The filing also says that after Alfozan's arrest, his iPhone was found to contain photographs dated Sept. 22 to 28 depicting "at least one additional concealed device as well as what appear to be the input/output panels on televisions and other electronic devices in various locations in OpenAI buildings, including another conference room where sensitive meetings frequently occurred." "The defendant's residence contained several electronic components similar to those in the customized devices the defendant installed in the OpenAI conference room," the filing said. OpenAI also found another recording device in a bag Alfozan inadvertently left behind in a printer room on Oct. 5, the same day he was seen on camera checking behind the TV where the first recording device had been left in the conference room, prosecutors have said. headlines.article_text: JPMorgan's $5 billion bet on U.S. security; startups Castelion, Hadrian Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points JPMorgan Chase has deployed $5 billion into startup investments in the first year of its U.S. security and resiliency initiative, halfway to its initial $10 billion goal. The bank may exceed that target, co-President Doug Petno told CNBC. JPMorgan has taken stakes in startups Hadrian, which builds automated factories for aerospace and defense firms, and Castelion, which is developing low-cost hypersonic missiles. Separately, JPMorgan has financed and facilitated more than $230 billion in transactions in the initiative's first year, part of a broader goal of supporting $1.5 trillion in activity over a decade. In this article JPM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The head of JPMorgan Chase's new security and resiliency initiative, Todd Combs, then portfolio manager at Berkshire Hathaway Inc., is seen at Berkshire Hathaway's shareholders meeting in Omaha, Nebraska, May 4, 2014. Daniel Acker / Bloomberg / Getty Images JPMorgan Chase has made $5 billion in startup investments in the first year of its U.S. security and resiliency initiative , the company said Monday, a faster-than-expected pace that indicates the bank is finding plentiful opportunities in emerging defense, manufacturing and supply chain firms. The bank, which last year said it would deploy $10 billion into startups over a decade, may expand the program beyond that initial dollar amount, JPMorgan co-President Doug Petno told CNBC in an interview. Todd Combs, the former Berkshire Hathaway executive who leads the JPMorgan group in charge of making startup investments , has "hit the ground running," Petno said. "He's done a great job and put us in some really interesting companies," he added. Most of those investments have yet to be disclosed, but two known stakes seem emblematic of the project's mission to bolster companies that are needed for a more dangerous and chaotic era of geopolitics. JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets, has taken direct stakes in defense-related startups Hadrian and Castelion . Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as trade disputes with China, have threatened the flow of energy and key components needed for U.S. industries and defense, which spurred JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon into creating the initiative a year ago. He put Petno, widely seen as one of two key possible successors , in charge of the overall investment project. Combs, a former board member of the bank, reports directly to Dimon. The scope of the project extends beyond supply chain, defense and manufacturing to include frontier technologies and the pharmaceutical and health-tech industries. Troy Rohrbaugh and Douglas Petno, co-CEOs of Commercial & Investment Bank at JPMorganChase. Courtesy: JPMorganChase "There's a lot of really interesting companies that have been working to solve some of these problems," Petno said. These "early venture-stage, advanced manufacturing companies have found ways to build these capabilities in the U.S." rather than relying on overseas trading partners, he said. In August, the bank helped lead a $1.4 billion funding round for Hadrian, which builds automated factories that make parts for the defense, aerospace and maritime sectors. A California factory run by Hadrian has 10 robots for every human employee, according to the startup's founder. That month, JPMorgan was also involved in a $1 billion funding round for Castelion, whose flagship product is a relatively low-cost hypersonic missile called Blackbeard. Castelion was founded in late 2022 by a group of former SpaceX engineers. "Our approach is to find generational companies and partner with them for the long term," Combs said in a statement Monday. "Putting more than $5 billion to work in our first year shows how many exceptional businesses are building in industries that strengthen critical supply chains," Combs said. Risky business? JPMorgan making billions of dollars of direct investments in nascent companies is a departure from its usual role as a lender and advisor. Before the defense initiative, the bank had moved away from taking startup stakes, which can be relatively risky bets on unproven technologies. JPMorgan spun off its private equity business, One Equity Partners, more than a decade ago. In its more traditional role, JPMorgan has also financed and facilitated more than $230 billion for industries that support American national interests, according to the bank. That part of its security and resiliency project, meant to hit $1.5 trillion over 10 years, is led by Jay Horine , a former co-head of investment banking. JPMorgan built a team for the project of about three dozen bankers, who are aided by hundreds more across the firm, as it expanded the initiative to Europe and Canada. Its bankers are mapping distribution lines for key products, from submarines and missiles to aircraft, to identify suppliers that may lack the capital or capacity to meet rising demand, according to Petno. headlines.article_text: Elon Musk says he'll give a SpaceX share to every child in U.S. Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points SpaceX boss Elon Musk said Monday that he'll give one of his shares in the company to every child in the U.S. next year. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 3:00 03:00 Elon Musk to give away one SpaceX share to every American child next year Squawk Box Europe SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said Monday that he'll give every child in the U.S. one of his shares in the company next year. Musk currently owns about 4.8 billion SpaceX shares, according to an August SEC filing. That figure rises to 6.4 billion when taking into account unvested awards and stock options, representing a 48.4% beneficial stake in the company. There were 72 million children under 18 in the U.S. as of July 1, 2025, according to official census data. That would amount to the CEO giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, taking into account SpaceX's closing stock price of $146.03 as of Friday. "This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X, without providing further details on how the share giveaway would happen. CNBC has reached out to SpaceX for further comment. Musk's financial giving has been in the news in recent weeks primarily for his political contributions. The Tesla CEO has spent more than $276 million in donations to Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election. The world's richest person poured $158 million into the Senate Leadership Fund, the Republican Party's leading Senate super PAC, in September through an affiliated Texas PAC created to support Republican Ken Paxton. Musk's two contributions of $75 million and $83 million are among the largest political donations ever. Musk's post came hot on the heels of Anthropic revealing that it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows. In response to an Anthropic post on X about the fund on Sunday, Musk replied, "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," and added that's what he'd be doing. Subject to shareholder approval, Anthropic's fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed. The fund may be used to "explore large donations," including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations, or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said. — CNBC's Jennifer Liu contributed to this report. The range is more in line with BB and B credit, which is high yield, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence. The spread on Oracle's five-year CDS is currently 295 basis points, after briefly hitting 300 bps on Thursday, up 287% in one year. "Oracle CDS is supported by high liquidity. Nonetheless, its spreads whipsawed over the last few days, no doubt a reflection of the fragile sentiment in AI-related names, notably those in HY [high yield] and at the weaker end of the IG [investment-grade] spectrum, such as Oracle," he said in an email to CNBC. Oracle's 5-year credit default swaps Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CDS means investors view the debt as riskier. Oracle's rating is S&P Credit Ratings is BBB-, the lowest level in the investment-grade spectrum. The agency downgraded Oracle in July, noting that the company's rapidly expanding infrastructure business is increasing its overall credit risk. S&P also said it expects weaker operating cash flow in 2027. A 'bellwether' Oracle is primarily an enterprise software company but it's barreling into data centers and cloud services, including a massive $300 billion deal with OpenAI. To fund the buildout, Oracle has issued $118 billion in long-term debt and has another $39 billion in capital and lease obligations, according to FactSet data. The spending and debt obligations are taking a toll on Oracle's finances while the company waits for a gusher of AI revenue. Analysts estimate free cash flow of -$23.7 billion this year and -$36 billion in 2027, according to consensus forecasts. That would be bad enough for investors, but Oracle is more than just a debt-laden data center play. It's become an AI "bellwether," notes Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Deutsche Bank. A downgrade of its credit into junk territory "would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," he said in a report. S&P said in its July downgrade that another downgrade could be triggered by: an expectation that Oracle will sustain leverage exceeding 4x; or belief that the software company isn't on a path to generate positive free operating cash flow by fiscal 2029; or a negative view on Oracle's AI strategy or that of the overall AI industry. As an investment-grade company, Oracle can borrow cheaply and with duration, but that would change with a junk rating, said Jamie Meyers, a senior securities analyst at Laffer Tengler, which owns Oracle stock. "Nobody in high yield is going to buy a 30 year debt," he said. "Getting downgraded to junk would mean that they'd have to push everything short. Obviously, their borrowing rate would be higher, more than likely." That said, Meyers is not concerned about Oracle's debt levels. In a meeting between Oracle and Laffer Tengler last year, Oracle stressed it will defend its investment-grade rating, Meyers said. "We do believe the revenue is going to start ramping and the earnings are going to start ramping," he said. "What Oracle really needs is … time. They need to get these things built." Brad Collins, a fixed income portfolio manager at Vanguard, also expressed confidence in Oracle and the other hyperscalers. "Oracle is most under the microscope, but as a result, has been more diligent in their issuance" so far this year, he said. "Balance sheets are in a healthy starting spot, and [I] would not extrapolate what we are seeing in HY to IG." The company's current troubles could be looked at as a "financing test," said Dynasty Financial Partners' Nerney. They'll either pass or fail, which could mean an additional downgrade, he said. "The real question now is, with the move in rates, how much is that going to cost?" he said. "If rates continue to move higher, just the opportunity cost of investors to hold Oracle paper relative to other things in the market, you're going to see the market demand more." Oracle responded to a request for comment by saying, "We have been very clear that maintaining an investment grade rating is our first priority as a company." "The AI infrastructure business has strong economic returns and we expect it will produce strong free cash flows once projects are ramped," it added.
